issues: Both quotes are verbatim (FOUND), and all three values match their sources: 2,700 in 1950 (Themenmappe 1), 'rund 16.000' in 1956 and 91,015 at 31.10.1989 (MfS-Lexikon). The Themenmappe imprint 'Berlin 2022' confirms the date. The Lexikon entry is signed by Jens Gieseke.

Precision issue on the 1950 point. It is marked estimate: false, but 2,700 is a rounded year-end figure. German Wikipedia, citing Gieseke in Dümmel/Piepenschneider (eds.), Was war die Stasi? (KAS 2014), p. 68, says: 'Bis Ende des Jahres beschäftigte das neu gegründete Ministerium bereits rund 2700 Mitarbeiter' (FOUND). The MfS was founded on 8 February 1950 (law in force 21 February), so the 1950 point is an end-of-year figure of 'about' 2,700, not a founding-day strength. The point is now marked as an estimate with a note.

Clarity for readers: 'hauptamtliche Mitarbeiter' is broader than career officers. The same Themenmappe gives the 1989 make-up as about 79% career officers and NCOs, 14% fixed-term NCOs and soldiers, 2.5% officers on special assignment (OibE), 2.3% full-time unofficial collaborators and 0.2% civilian staff (FOUND). The Lexikon says the fixed-term soldiers served mainly in the Feliks Dzierzynski guard regiment. This is added to the notes so the 91,015 is not read as 91,000 spies.

No other problems. The Lexikon's 'Am stärksten wuchs der Stasi-Apparat von 1968 bis 1982' (FOUND) confirms that the three points must not be joined by a straight line as if growth were linear; the existing notes already warn that intermediate years were not read.

fieldFixes.notes: Three verified points only; intermediate years exist in Gieseke (2000) but were not read. Growth was not linear: the MfS-Lexikon says the apparatus grew fastest from 1968 to 1982, so do not interpolate. 1950 is an approximate year-end figure (the ministry was founded on 8 February 1950); 1956 is 'rund' (about) 16,000; 1989 is the exact count at 31 October 1989. 'Full-time staff' includes, in 1989, about 79% career officers and NCOs, 14% fixed-term NCOs and soldiers (chiefly the Feliks Dzierzynski guard regiment), 2.5% officers on special assignment (OibE), 2.3% full-time unofficial collaborators and 0.2% civilian employees (Bundesarchiv Themenmappe 1).

issues: Wrong year. The trial was in 1889, not 1888. The Census Bureau's own history, Leon E. Truesdell's The Development of Punch Card Tabulation in the Bureau of the Census 1890-1940 (GPO 1965), pp. 40-42, has a section headed 'The 1889 test'. It says that 'In compliance with a suggestion made by the Secretary of the Interior in 1889, the Superintendent of the Census, Robert P. Porter, appointed a committee', and that 'The report of the committee, dated November 30, 1889, describes the test' (both FOUND). Porter was superintendent only from 1889. The '1888' on census.gov (and on IBM's heritage page, which copies census.gov) is an error; the letalone-1 verdict on hollerith-punch-cards-1890-census-1890 found the same.

Wrong value for the second contestant. census.gov gives 100.5 hours, but Truesdell's table of the test records gives 110 h 56 min. The OCR row reads '110 [OCR: no] 56 | 44 41 | 155 37', and the row total proves it: 110:56 + 44:41 = 155:37, while 100:56 + 44:41 would be 145:37. The other rows also add up: Hollerith 72:27 + 5:28 = 77:55, and 144:25 + 55:22 = 199:47. The table check is FOUND. So the values should be 144.4 (144 h 25 min), 110.9 (110 h 56 min) and 72.5 (72 h 27 min). census.gov's 144.5 and 72.5 are roundings; its 100.5 is not.

Wrong pairing in the notes. 'Sorting times were 44.5, 55.5 and 5.5 hours respectively' pairs 44.5 with the 144.5-hour contestant. Truesdell's rows pair 55 h 22 min with the 144 h 25 min system and 44 h 41 min with the 110 h 56 min system. Hollerith's tabulation time was 5 h 28 min, and Truesdell notes the test table was 'barely enough for one run of the cards'. Also, 'sorting' is not the source's term: Truesdell has 'To tabulate' and census.gov 'prepare data for tabulation'.

Missing context, now added: the rivals were William C. Hunt's card or slip system and Charles F. Pidgin's chip system (both FOUND in Truesdell). The OCR'd table has lost its row labels, so the page must not say which rival took 144 or 110 hours. The test used four enumeration districts of St. Louis, 'selected from the re-enumeration of 1880', with 10,491 inhabitants (FOUND). The geography and label are updated.
The source's date is wrong: the census.gov page footer says 'Last Revised - August 14, 2024', not 2026.

The id keeps '1888' for referential stability, but the label, notes and point years must say 1889. Cross-record flag: the event hollerith-punch-cards-1890-census-1890 (and the letalone-1 fixed summary) still says the rivals needed '144.5 and 100.5 hours'. The 100.5 should become about 111 hours (110 h 56 min) there too.

fieldFixes.label: 1889 Census Office test: hours to transcribe 1880 St. Louis census returns onto cards or chips, by system
fieldFixes.geography: Four enumeration districts of St. Louis, Missouri (10,491 inhabitants; returns from the 1880 re-enumeration)
fieldFixes.notes: Not a time series: all three points are the same test, whose committee report is dated 30 November 1889 (Truesdell 1965, pp. 40-42). Census Bureau and IBM web pages date it 1888 and give the middle rival as 100.5 hours; Truesdell's table (110 h 56 min + 44 h 41 min = 155 h 37 min total) shows 110 h 56 min. Value is transcription time (schedules to punched cards, written cards or chips). Tabulation times were 55 h 22 min (for the 144 h 25 min system), 44 h 41 min (for the 110 h 56 min system) and 5 h 28 min (Hollerith). The rivals were William C. Hunt's slip system and Charles F. Pidgin's chip system; the OCR'd table does not show which row is which.
